Hi Alex, thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned.

Call recap (high level):
- Targets: p95 latency ~150ms, p99 <= 300ms for single-turn generate requests.
- Throughput / concurrency: steady-state ~1k concurrent requests (average), normal sustained RPS ~600; need to handle marketing-driven bursts up to ~5k concurrent (peak) and the rare promotional spike ~10k for ~2-3 minutes.
- Streaming: yes; user sessions stream partial responses (token-by-token) and we need sub-200ms first-byte in steady-state for good UX.
- Failure tolerance / queueing: prefer soft-queueing with backpressure vs hard rejects; SLO is 99.5% success under expected load.
- Warm pools / scale-up: desire <45s effective scale-up to serve burst traffic without user-visible degradation.

Attachments: I've attached a first-pass SLO matrix (slo_matrix_v1.xlsx) and our notes on autoscale behaviors (autoscale_design_notes.pdf).

Proposed next steps:
1) Alex, can you share a 7-day traffic profile (by minute) and a sample of streaming session characteristics (avg tokens/sec, avg session length)? That will help our qualification test.
2) I'll loop in Dylan (SE) to propose a warm-pool + reserved-capacity design and a PoC plan for SLO qualification.
3) We'll run a focused SLO qualification PoC against a synthetic replay of your traffic + a marketing burst scenario.

Can we aim to schedule the deep technical session next Tuesday or Wednesday? I'll propose times.

Thanks,

Thanks Marissa, this is great, appreciate the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Traffic profile: we have steady-state payments-matching flows that sit around 600 RPS during US business hours. Marketing/event-driven spikes are the pain point; last year a campaign produced a burst that peaked at ~10k requests for ~3 minutes, then decayed back to baseline. Bursts are short but intense.
- Streaming: sessions are typically 8-12 minutes; token throughput varies but first-byte latency is what our product team cares about most.
- Concurrency: many of those burst requests are short-lived (single-turn) but can still create a concurrency spike.
- Pre-warm requirement: if we can pre-warm capacity ahead of an expected campaign we can avoid most issues, but we need an approach that also protects us against unexpected spikes.

I'll attach a small traffic snapshot and anonymized session sample (traffic_snapshot.json), this should help.

Thanks for the quick details, Alex, that snapshot is exactly what we need for sizing. Looping in Dylan (SE) to propose two short options:

Option A, Reserved baseline + warm pool:
- Reserve capacity sized for ~1k concurrent requests (steady state).
- Maintain a small warm pool (idle but warmed GPUs) that can absorb a 5x burst with <45s latency impact.
- Use predictive pre-warm hooks for scheduled campaigns (you can trigger via an API or calendar integration).

Option B, Hybrid reserved + elastic burst:
- Baseline reserved for normal traffic, elastic for rare large spikes (10k).
- Elastic nodes spin up within 30-90s depending on instance type; combine with short soft-queueing and fast-fallback to smaller models for degraded conditions.

Questions for PE team / PoC scope:
- Desired PoC SLA targets (we recommend targeting p95 150ms / p99 300ms).
- Specific burst profile to test (Alex's snapshot + one synthetic 10k 3-minute spike).

Dylan, can you draft a short playbook for warm-pool sizing (CPU/GPU mix, expected scale-up times) and a PoC test plan?

I'll pencil in Tuesday 2pm PT for the deep-dive unless that doesn't work.

Best,
Marissa

Hi Alex / Marissa, quick technical note and proposed warm-pool approach. See attached autoscale_playbook.md for details.

Short version:
- Warm pool strategy: keep a configurable set of warmed workers (small GPU-backed instances) that hold model artifacts in memory and have KV caches populated for top-traffic prefixes. Warm pool should absorb the first 30-60s of a burst while elastic nodes spin up.
- Scale-up times: based on our benchmarks, cold spin-up for a full node + model load is ~45-90s depending on quantization and model size; warm pool entry is ~5-15s.
- Queueing behavior: recommend a soft queue with exponential backoff + token-bucket rate limiter per-customer to avoid head-of-line blocking. For user-facing streams, return partial results if tail latency exceeds threshold and escalate to fallback smaller model.
- Autoscale warm heuristics: pre-warm triggers (calendar API / manual API call) + traffic-based predictive scaling using the last 5min window. For unknown spikes, combining conservative soft-queueing with cached short-lived workers gives best UX.
- PoC plan: replay Alex's 7-day profile, then run two burst tests (5k sustained for 3m and 10k spike for 3m). We'll measure p95/p99 latency, first-byte streaming latency, and request success rate.

I'll include concrete instance sizing and a step-by-step PoC runbook in the attached.
